item.title: Can Israel’s Opposition Unseat Netanyahu?
item.description:
More than two weeks after one of the most consequential elections in Israel’s history, there is still uncertainty about who will lead the country.

The spotlight has fallen on the opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who is trying to make all kinds of deals to build a coalition that could run the government.

David Halbfinger, The New York Times’s Jerusalem bureau chief, explains the compromises that Mr. Eisenkot will need to make, and what will happen if he can’t.

Guest: David M. Halbfinger, the Jerusalem bureau chief for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Who is Gadi Eisenkot, the Israeli tasked with forming a government?
  • Here’s how Mr. Eisenkot is seeking to oust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Photo: Amir Levy/Getty Images

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: What Jensen Huang’s Resignation Will Mean for A.I.
item.description:
This episode was recorded before the news of Mr. Huang’s resignation was made public.

Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive of Nvidia on Thursday after The New York Times reported that he had extramarital relationships with a woman identified by U.S. officials as a Chinese spy and an executive at the company. In a memo this week, Mr. Huang admitted to being “unfaithful” to his wife.

Tripp Mickle, a tech reporter for The Times, discusses how everything unraveled for Mr. Huang and what his exit could mean for his and Nvidia’s future.

Guest: Tripp Mickle, a tech reporter for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia after news of his affairs was made public.
  • Nvidia shares plunged, shaking up tech stocks as Mr. Huang stepped down from his role.

Photo: Manuel Orbegozo for The New York Times

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: Public Schools Have a New Crisis: Not Enough Students
item.description:
The number of students in America’s public schools is shrinking. In some cases, the declines have been so drastic that districts are facing empty classrooms, painful budget cuts and angry debates about whether to close schools.

Sarah Mervosh, an education reporter at The New York Times, discusses what the enrollment crisis looks like, why it’s happening and how one school district hopes to fix it.

Guest: Sarah Mervosh, an education reporter at The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • American schools are facing a crisis as the number of children drops.
  • Why U.S. test scores are in a “generation-long decline.”

Photo: Erin Schaff/The New York Times

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: Secrets, Chips and Spycraft: The Nvidia C.E.O. Scandal
item.description:
Over the weekend, Jensen Huang, the chief executive and co-founder of Nvidia — which makes the chips that power artificial intelligence — admitted to having an affair with a woman who has been determined by U.S. officials to be a spy. That revelation came after The New York Times broke the story of how U.S. intelligence officers uncovered what they say was a plot by Alice Huang to use their relationship to funnel information to Beijing.

Tripp Mickle, a White House correspondent for The Times, explains how Beijing tried to compromise one of the tech executives closest to President Trump, and what the scandal could mean for a company with enormous influence over the future of A.I. — and the entire American economy.

Guest: Tripp Mickle, a tech reporter for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Jensen Huang’s tight grip on Nvidia presents a challenge for the company’s board, which is investigating his affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.
  • Mr. Huang acknowledged having had a relationship with a business executive who U.S. officials determined was working for Chinese intelligence.

Photo: Manuel Orbegozo/Reuters

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: After a Crushing Defeat, Trump Doubles Down
item.description:
After a stinging rebuke last week at the polls, President Trump announced that he would elevate Stephen Miller — a driving force behind some of the most polarizing policies of Mr. Trump’s second term — to chief of staff.

Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, White House reporters for The New York Times, explain what Mr. Miller’s appointment reveals about the president’s priorities for his final two years in office.

Guests: 

  • Maggie Haberman, a White House correspondent for The New York Times.
  • Jonathan Swan, a White House reporter for The New York Times.

Background reading: After midterm election losses, the Republican Party has entered its most uncertain moment in years.

The new chief of staff is poised to push the limits of the president’s power.

Photo: Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: Introducing ‘METRO’ From Serial Productions
item.description:
Today, we’re sharing an episode from a brand-new show called “METRO,” made by the Serial podcast team and the reporters here at The Times who cover New York City.


Every other week, Sarah Koenig and her team will tell stories about the city and its most fascinating raw material: New Yorkers. They’ll bring you investigations, personal stories, essays and interviews that take the bigness of New York and make it human scale and relevant, no matter where you live. 
 

You can find all episodes of Serial’s “METRO” wherever you get your podcasts and in The New York Times app.

item.title: Chuck Schumer on Governing With (Or Without) Trump
item.description:
Warning: This episode contains strong language.

Last spring, the political picture for Senator Chuck Schumer, the minority leader, was downright bleak. President Trump was back in the White House. Schumer’s Democratic caucus was largely powerless to stop him. And restless Democratic activists were calling for Schumer to resign.

Fast forward to this week. Democrats have roared back to power in both the Senate, where the party flipped seven Republican seats, and the House. And now Schumer, who personally recruited several of the winning candidates, is poised to become the next Senate majority leader with an unambiguous goal: reining in Trump.

On Thursday afternoon, I visited Schumer’s office in the U.S. Capitol to talk about all of that during a 45-minute interview. In between profanity-laced descriptions of the president, Schumer laid out his plans for Senate Democrats over the next two years, including investigations into the Trump administration and legislation seeking to lower Americans’ cost of living.

Guest: Chuck Schumer, the Senate Minority leader.

Photo: Alex Kent/The New York Times

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

Last spring, the political picture for Senator Chuck Schumer, the minority leader, was downright bleak. President Trump was back in the White House. Schumer’s Democratic caucus was largely powerless to stop him. And restless Democratic activists were calling for Schumer to resign.
Fast forward to this week. Democrats have roared back to power in both the Senate, where the party flipped seven Republican seats, and the House. And now Schumer, who personally recruited several of the winning candidates, is poised to become the next Senate majority leader with an unambiguous goal: reining in Trump.
On Thursday afternoon, I visited Schumer’s office in the U.S. Capitol to talk about all of that during a 45-minute interview. In between profanity-laced descriptions of the president, Schumer laid out his plans for Senate Democrats over the next two years, including investigations into the Trump administration and legislation seeking to lower Americans’ cost of living.

item.title: The Voters Who Flipped Congress
item.description:
The midterm elections were an electoral tsunami for Democrats: a complete collapse of the Republican coalition and a landslide victory.

Nate Cohn, the chief political analyst for The New York Times, examines the results to figure out which voters showed up, which stayed home and how much billions in campaign spending mattered.

Guest: Nate Cohn, the chief political analyst for The New York Times.

Background Reading

  • There’s no modern precedent for this Democratic tsunami.
  • Trump is confronting an identity he would rather not: a lame duck.

Photo: Nicole Craine for The New York Times

item.title: A Landslide Victory for Democrats
item.description:
On Tuesday night, the blue wave that polls predicted landed with extraordinary force across the United States as Democrats flipped control of both the House and the Senate.

Nate Cohn, Lisa Lerer and Shane Goldmacher of The New York Times discuss an extraordinary shift in power and a new era of American politics.

Guest: 

  • Nate Cohn, the chief political analyst for The New York Times.
  • Lisa Lerer, a national political correspondent for The New York Times.
  • Shane Goldmacher, a national political correspondent for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Democrats seized control of Congress as voters rebuked President Trump.
  • A Democratic rout stunned Texas in a seismic shift that was once unthinkable.

Photo: Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times

item.title: A Political Rebellion in the Rio Grande Valley
item.description:
Warning: This episode contains strong language.

In the midterm elections, one of the regions expected to swing away from President Trump and toward Democrats is the Rio Grande Valley of Texas, where life has been transformed by his administration’s crackdown on immigration.

Lynsea Garrison, a producer for “The Daily,” has been reporting on that shift and on the unlikely group leading the charge.

Guest: Lynsea Garrison, a senior producer on “The Daily.”

Background reading: 

  • Hispanic voters on the Texas border have soured on Mr. Trump.

item.title: Want to Enjoy Music More? Go For a Run.
item.description:
Ben Ratliff, a music critic and avid runner, always ran in silence. Then he discovered how music opened up to him — while running. It changed his entire approach to criticism and listening. He calls it “running the song.”

Today, for the New York City Marathon, Ben talks with our host Rachel Abrams about how his listening sharpens when he runs to music.

Then, he goes through highlights from his five-hour New York City Marathon playlist, which is designed to complement a run through the five boroughs, featuring various styles of music connected to the places on the route.

On Today’s Episode

  • Ben Ratliff, a former New York Times music critic, a music professor and the author of “Run the Song: Writing About Running About Listening.”

Background Listening

  • Ben Ratliff’s New York City Marathon playlist

Photo: Karsten Moran for The New York Times

item.title: The Art of the Pardon: How Trump Turned Clemency Into a Business
item.description:
In the final stretch of the midterm election campaign, polls have found that voters are latching onto the perceived corruption of the Trump administration.

Kenneth P. Vogel, a New York Times investigative journalist, explores one major story line feeding that perception: how those around the president have turned the pardon process into a business.

Guest: Kenneth P. Vogel, an investigative journalist for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • The pardon industry offers rich offenders a path to President Trump.
  • A billionaire wanted a pardon from Mr. Trump. His family gave Alina Habba a $50 million deal.

Photo: Tierney L. Cross/The New York Times

item.title: A Plan for Two Dans: How Democrats Manipulated Alaska’s Ballot
item.description:
An investigation from The New York Times has uncovered how two candidates named Dan Sullivan ended up on the ballot for U.S. Senate in Alaska and the secret role that Democrats played in making it happen.

Kellen Browning, a political reporter for The Times, takes us inside the political scheme and explains what it means for a race that could determine which party controls the Senate.

Guest: Kellen Browning, a political reporter for The New York Times in San Francisco.

Background reading: 

  • Inside Democrats’ secret effort to stack Alaska’s ballot.
  • After The Times’s article, the governor of Alaska ordered an investigation into Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign over its role in recruiting spoiler candidates.
  • Previously, the Justice Department asked a federal court to block Alaska’s results if the Republican incumbent narrowly lost.

Photo: Haven Daley/Associated Press

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: Is Running From Trump Enough to Save Republicans on Tuesday?
item.description:
A look at candidates from President Trump’s party who are running on a platform of criticizing him. 

In next week’s midterm elections, a specific kind of Republican candidate is appealing to disillusioned voters of both parties: moderates willing to criticize President Trump.

Jess Bidgood explains how some Republicans are trying to bring back an older version of their party.

Guest: Jess Bidgood, a political journalist for The New York Times

Background reading: 

  • A Trump backlash endangers Susan Collins, the only blue-state Republican senator.
  • From Opinion: John E. Sununu is running a model campaign. He might still lose.

item.title: They Protested ICE. Now They’ve Been Convicted of Terrorism.
item.description:
On July 4, 2025, a group of 10 antifa protesters was arrested, accused of what the federal government called a planned attack on the Prairieland detention facility in Texas. They were prosecuted as terrorists.

Janet Reitman, who has been covering the story, discusses the legal case and the questions it raises about who now qualifies as a terrorist in America.

Guest: Janet Reitman, who writes for The New York Times Magazine.

Background reading: 

  • Inside the group of Texans accused of being antifa terrorists.

Photo: Juan Figueroa/The Dallas Morning News, via Getty Images

item.title: The $10 Billion Midterm Ad War
item.description:
The midterms are shaping up to be the most expensive election cycle in history as campaigns pour huge sums into the ads voters see virtually everywhere.

Today, Shane Goldmacher, a national political correspondent for The New York Times, breaks down how Democrats are tying Republicans to President Trump, inflation and corruption, while Republicans are trying to paint Democrats as too liberal. He also weighs in on what those competing messages reveal about each party’s hopes, vulnerabilities and strategy as Election Day nears.

Guest: Shane Goldmacher, a national political correspondent for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Mr. Trump has wielded an unprecedented $277 million in the final stretch of the midterms.
  • Both parties are spending enormous amounts of money to try to win whatever votes are left for the taking before Election Day.
  • Mr. Trump’s super PAC is flooding Facebook and Instagram with targeted ads as it seeks to turn out Republicans amid the president’s historically low approval ratings.

Photo: Kenny Holston/The New York Times

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: Tricks, Treats and Trends
item.description:
Americans are expected to spend a record $13.5 billion on Halloween this year, according to the National Retail Federation. That includes costumes, decorations and lots of candy.

In this episode of “The Sunday Daily,” our host Rachel Abrams talks about these three tent poles of the Halloween season with reporters from across the Times newsroom.

Kim Severson, who covers food, tells us about the sour, peelable and texture-confused candy edging out longtime chocolate favorites. Louis Lucero II, an editor for style coverage, predicts the most popular costumes of the year. And Callie Holtermann, a reporter who covers style and pop culture, discusses the enduring joy of “Skelly,” the 12-foot-tall Home Depot skeleton with a cult following.

On Today’s Episode:

Kim Severson covers all aspects of food culture for The New York Times.

Louis Lucero II, an editor for style coverage for The New York Times.

Callie Holtermann, a reporter who writes about style, pop culture and Gen Z for The New York Times.

Background Reading:

  • Halloween Costume Ideas That Scream 2026
  • Still the Biggest Skeleton In the Game?

item.title: The Battle Over Black Representation in the South
item.description:
The approach to this year’s midterms has brought two hugely consequential changes to voting for Black Americans: the gutting of the Voting Rights Act, and redistricting. In the wake of those actions, efforts are underway to mobilize Black voters in the South.

In Mississippi, the Senate battle is being seen as a sleeper race, and the Black Democrat running has a chance of flipping the seat, but state lawmakers are trying to redraw the maps and do away with their one majority Black district.

Today, Emily Cochrane, a reporter covering the American South for The New York Times, addresses the implications for voters across the region — not just in the midterms, but for years to come.

Guest: Emily Cochrane, a national reporter for The New York Times covering the American South.

Background reading: 

  • Black Democratic candidates running in the South have implored Black voters to go to the polls in response to the gutting of the Voting Rights Act.
  • High-profile Democrats across the country have some hope in Scott Colom’s bid for a seat in the Senate.

Photo: Anna Foley/The New York Times

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: The Election That Will Define Israel’s Future
item.description:
Israelis head to the polls next week. On the ballot is the future of a country that has become isolated on the world stage, because of both its war in Gaza and a growing outcry over settler violence in the West Bank.

David M. Halbfinger, the Jerusalem bureau chief for The New York Times, explains how Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu differs from his biggest challenger.

Background reading:

item.title: James Talarico on the Rage Economy, Billionaires and Flipping Texas
item.description:
James Talarico is asking Texas to do something it hasn’t done in nearly 40 years: Elect a Democrat to the U.S. Senate. It won’t be easy. It will take a vast coalition of Democrats, independents and Republicans in a bright red state that President Trump won by about 14 percentage points in 2024 — and where Republicans have plowed hundreds of millions of dollars into beating Mr. Talarico. And yet, poll after poll shows that Mr. Talarico could pull it off and defeat his Republican rival, Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general and a Trump ally. 

On Monday, nearly two weeks before Election Day, Michael Barbaro spoke with Mr. Talarico about the kind of race he’s running, why it has succeeded so far in appealing to Republicans and what he wants Democrats to do if they flip control of the Senate on Nov. 3.

Guest: James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas.

Background reading: 

  • Top Democrats, who have long been hesitant to spend money in Texas, have started to back Mr. Talarico.

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: Inside Putin’s Plan to Cripple Ukraine This Winter
item.description:
President Trump said he was making an energy deal with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and waiving new sanctions on Moscow. Now, he’s feuding with Ukraine’s leader, Volodymyr Zelensky.

Russia is taking advantage of the moment by relentlessly striking Kyiv, killing civilians and cutting off power for more than a million people.

Constant Méheut, who is covering the war for The New York Times, explains why Mr. Putin appears so confident that Russia can bomb Ukraine into submission.

Guest: Constant Méheut, a correspondent covering the war in Ukraine for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Analysis: Why Russia sees a window to bomb Ukraine into submission.
  • Mr. Zelensky says Mr. Trump risks a “historic mistake” if he backs Russia.

item.title: Elizabeth Holmes and Nathan Fielder Keep Us Guessing
item.description:
The comedian Nathan Fielder came to fame as the creator and host of the Comedy Central series “Nathan for You.” The show followed Fielder as he devised outrageous schemes, ostensibly with the aim of helping various small businesses. What became clear, though, was that Fielder was less interested in helping business owners generate profits than he was in understanding the people ensnared in his plots. His next project, the HBO series “The Rehearsal,” was a similar offbeat portrait of offbeat people. At the center of both projects is Fielder himself, a documentarian whose motives can sometimes be hard to parse.

This week, Fielder’s first feature-length documentary, “You Can See Everything,” hits theaters. Co-directed by Lance Oppenheim, the movie shows Fielder embedding himself into the life of the disgraced Theranos founder and felon Elizabeth Holmes in the days leading up to her imprisonment for fraud. The film caused a big splash when it debuted at the Telluride Film Festival, in part because it presents Holmes, a mysterious and compelling cultural figure, through the eyes of Fielder, a mysterious and compelling filmmaker.

This week, the Times movie critic Alissa Wilkinson and critic at large Jason Zinoman, who covers comedy, join Michael Barbaro for a spoiler-free discussion of Nathan Fielder, his career, and why he might be the perfect person to tell the story of Elizabeth Holmes.

 

On Today’s Episode

Alissa Wilkinson, a movie critic at The New York Times.

Jason Zinoman, a critic at large for the Culture section of The New York Times.

 

Background Reading

  • ‘The Real World’ and Nathan Fielder can both thank this cult filmmaker.
  • ‘You Can See Everything,’ if you could only secure a ticket.

 

Photo: A24, via Associated Press

item.title: MAGA's Midterm Defectors
item.description:
Perhaps no American feels the domestic effects of the war, tariffs and inflation more than the Iowa farmer. The political environment stirred up by those farmers’ strife could allow the Democrats to seize the moment and elect one of theirs to the Senate or the governor’s mansion for the first time in 20 years — making Iowa potentially one of the most important states on the map this midterm cycle.

Today, we follow Caleb Renner, a young farmer in north central Iowa, as he shows the effects of the past two years on his community and talks about why those effects may lead him to turn on the Republican Party for the first time, and whether that will translate into support for Democrats.

Guest: Caleb Renner, a farmer in Klemme, Iowa.

Background reading: 

  • Who’s winning the race for Congress?
  • ‘Survival Mode Time’: Republicans accelerate their break with Trump.

Photo: KC McGinnis for The New York Times

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: The Republican Strategy to Salvage the Midterms
item.description:
With Republicans trailing in the polls, the party is making hard choices about where to spend its money — abandoning some races while pouring resources into others.

Shane Goldmacher, Nate Cohn and Lisa Lerer, political correspondents for The New York Times, explain why President Trump is campaigning almost daily in deep-red territory, how his influence is shaping the strategy and whether Democrats can win over the disenchanted voters they may need to take back the House and the Senate.

Guests: 

  • Shane Goldmacher, a national political correspondent for The New York Times.
  • Nate Cohn, the chief political analyst for The New York Times.
  • Lisa Lerer, a national political correspondent for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Economic pain and an unpopular Trump have put the G.O.P. on its heels.
  • Top Republican groups are pulling support from two House incumbents.

Photo: Kenny Holston/The New York Times

item.title: The U.S. Tried to Choke Russia’s Energy Market. Then It Made a Diesel Deal.
item.description:
President Trump announced a deal to purchase Russian diesel fuel and temporarily suspended sanctions in an effort to lower domestic fuel prices amid rising costs from the war in Iran and in anticipation of the upcoming midterms. This abrupt foreign policy shift stunned European allies and drew sharp criticism from Ukraine, which viewed the move as a weakening of Western leverage against Russia.

Today, Anton Troianovski, a global affairs correspondent for The New York Times, discusses what the deal reveals about the Trump administration’s strategy with Russia, and how much it could actually lower prices at the pump.

Guest: Anton Troianovski, a global affairs correspondent for The New York Times who writes about foreign policy, national security and America’s place in the world.

Background reading: Trump faces a new crisis over Ukraine following the Russian diesel deal.

Photo: Igor Grussak/picture alliance via Getty Images

item.title: When A.I. Comes for Your Purpose in Life
item.description:
Artificial intelligence has gone from struggling with basic arithmetic to helping solve some of mathematics’ most famous open problems — and the field is reckoning with what that means.

Steven Strogatz, a professor of mathematics at Cornell University, describes the excitement and grief of watching A.I. take on work that gives people a sense of purpose — and asks what could be lost if machines deliver answers without the human struggle, insight and understanding that make solving problems meaningful.

Guest: Steven Strogatz, a professor of mathematics at Cornell University who writes for The New York Times about the future of research.

Background reading: 

  • Mathematics isn’t just a game to let A.I. solve — history shows why.
  • A.I. is mastering the kinds of projects that have long helped to build the careers of young mathematicians. What does that mean for their future?
  • Steven Strogatz’s forthcoming book: Big Math.

Photo: Ian C. Bates for The New York Times

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: The Israeli Film Directors Pushing for a Reckoning in Their Home Country
item.description:
The documentary film “NAZA,” which investigates the methods the Israeli military has used in the war in Gaza since the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, received a record-breaking standing ovation at the Venice Film Festival last month. Just a few days later, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he would propose legislation that could revoke the directors’ Israeli citizenship, arguing that they had defamed their country.

Now, with a global theatrical release underway, the directors spoke with “The Daily” to discuss the film and all the pushback that it — and they — have experienced.

Guest: 

  • Rachel Szor, an Israeli investigative journalist, film director and activist.
  • Yuval Abraham, an Israeli investigative journalist, film director and Arabic-Hebrew translator.

Background reading: 

  • After accolades abroad, “NAZA” met backlash at home.
  • Read The Times’s review of the film.

Photo: Stefano Rellandini/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images, The Guardian/IFC Center, Ander Gillenea/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

item.title: Celine Dion’s Triumphant Return to the Stage
item.description:
A dramatic pop music comeback story is underway: Celine Dion is performing again.

In 2022, Dion, the renowned Canadian singer, announced that she had stiff person syndrome, a rare and incurable neurological disorder that causes painful muscle spasms and affects roughly one in a million people. The announcement came as a shock to her fans, and in a raw and revealing documentary released in 2024, “I Am: Celine Dion," she shared her struggle to overcome her condition, and sing again. But Dion worked her way back to performing, and is now appearing in a run of sold out shows in Paris.

The culture reporter Elisabeth Vincentelli was there on opening night, and in this episode of “The Sunday Daily,” she talks with our host Natalie Kitroeff about the remarkable comeback of Celine Dion.

On Today’s Episode:

  • Elisabeth Vincentelli, an arts, culture, and theater journalist.

Background Reading:

  • Celine Dion Is Back Onstage. Naturally, She Chose Paris.
  • Paris Really, Really Loves Celine Dion

Photo credit: Clementine Schneidermann for The New York Times.

item.itunes:title: Celine Dion’s Triumphant Return to the Stage
item.itunes:author: The New York Times
item.itunes:summary:
A dramatic pop music comeback story is underway: Celine Dion is performing again.
In 2022, Dion, the renowned Canadian singer, announced that she had stiff person syndrome, a rare and incurable neurological disorder that causes painful muscle spasms and affects roughly one in a million people. The announcement came as a shock to her fans, and in a raw and revealing documentary released in 2024, “I Am: Celine Dion," she shared her struggle to overcome her condition, and sing again. But Dion worked her way back to performing, and is now appearing in a run of sold out shows in Paris.
The culture reporter Elisabeth Vincentelli was there on opening night, and in this episode of “The Sunday Daily,” she talks with our host Natalie Kitroeff about the remarkable comeback of Celine Dion.

item.title: Why France Is in Crisis
item.description:
For weeks, thousands of high school students in France have been out in the streets protesting the conditions of public schools. They want better funding, something that won’t be easy with the current state of French finances.

Mark Landler, the Paris bureau chief, explains why after years of overspending, France is in crisis, and is driving toward a fiscal cliff.

Guest: Mark Landler, the Paris bureau chief of The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • France’s debt problem is a warning to the world.
  • Understand the country’s polycrisis.
  • For the resurgent far left, the protests are an opening and a threat.

Photo: Miguel Medina/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

item.title: Three Vans, a Startled Farmer and an Iranian Plot Against the U.S.
item.description:
What exactly happened near an air base in Britain used by the United States?

Eric Schmitt, a national security correspondent for The New York Times, discusses what he’s learned about the mysterious events around the base, including the abrupt withdrawal of U.S. Air Force bombers.

Guest: Eric Schmitt, a national security correspondent for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • A mysterious call near a military base used by the United States set in motion a huge counterterrorism response and days of uncertainty in Britain.
  • The United States withdrew 12 bombers from the base after information emerged about a potential Iranian drone attack, U.S. and British officials said.

item.title: Call My A.I. Agent

Over the past few weeks, millions of people have rushed to download a new type of artificial intelligence app — agents. They are useful, kind of cute and need your most sensitive personal information to work.

item.title: Midterm Surprise: Democrats Are Surging in Red America
item.description:
A new set of polls from The New York Times finds that Democratic candidates are doing remarkably well in the Republican-leaning states that they need to win to gain control of the U.S. Senate in next month’s midterm elections.

They are doing less well in the blue states that, in theory, should be easier to win.

Nate Cohn, the chief political analyst for The Times, offers his idea of what is behind the numbers.

Guest: Nate Cohn, The New York Times’s chief political analyst.

Background reading: 

  • Polls suggested that Hispanic voters, whose support helped propel President Trump to the White House in 2024, would largely support the Democratic Party this time.
  • Senator Susan Collins of Maine led polls for the first time since Graham Platner dropped out of the race in July.

Photo: Ash Adams for The New York Times

item.title: The Restaurant Industry Is Broken. Can It Be Fixed?
item.description:
If you dine out regularly, you might have noticed some changes in restaurants over the past few years. Perhaps you’ve found yourself ordering at a counter, scanning a QR code to see the menu, or eating … a lot more soft serve.

These changes aren’t just trends. Brett Anderson, a New York Times food reporter, says they are restaurant owners’ desperate attempts to stay afloat in an industry in crisis. According to a report from the National Restaurant Association, 42 percent of restaurant owners said they weren’t profitable in 2025. Many of them were at serious risk of closing.

In this episode of “The Sunday Daily,” Brett talks with our host Michael Barbaro about the economic realities that are forcing businesses to rethink the entire concept of a restaurant, including a radical experiment at one Minneapolis diner that stopped charging for food entirely.

On Today’s Episode:

  • Brett Anderson, a reporter for the Food section of The New York Times.

Background Reading:

  • This Restaurant Stopped Charging for Food. And Profits Are Up.

  • The Restaurant List 2026

    Photo credit: Caroline Yang for The New York Times.

item.title: Why Washington Is Trying to Rein In College Sports
item.description:
In the five years since student athletes have been allowed to earn money, college sports have become a chaotic and murky marketplace where players can move from team to team chasing a payday.

Stewart Mandel of The Athletic explains why, this week, Washington decided to step in.

Guest: Stewart Mandel, the editor in chief of college football for The Athletic and a host of its college football podcast “The Audible.”

Background reading: 

  • The Protect College Sports Act wants to fix college sports. Here’s what it actually targets.
  • Does your college football roster cost $8 million or $50 million? Read The Athletic’s report on 68 teams.
  • Here’s how the football programs blow past limits on what they can pay players.

Photo: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

item.title: Inside the Devastating Hack of the F.B.I.
item.description:
A little over a decade ago, after hackers broke into the U.S. government and stole the personnel records of millions of federal workers, officials vowed that it would never happen again. Something similar recently did — to the F.B.I.

Dustin Volz, who covers cybersecurity for The New York Times, tells the story of the attack, the group behind it and what could happen to the stolen data.

Guest: Dustin Volz, a cybersecurity and intelligence reporter for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • The hackers said they had stolen thousands of sensitive F.B.I. personnel records.
  • The embarrassing breach at the F.B.I. has fueled fears of harm to its employees.

Photo: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Associated Press

item.title: Are Prediction Markets Gambling? A Lot Rides on the Answer.
item.description:
Prediction markets such as Kalshi and Polymarket have gained huge popularity over the past year. These marketplaces allow you to wager on just about anything — whether it’s who will win a football game or the weather in New York City.

David Yaffe-Bellany, a technology reporter for The New York Times, discusses the legal challenge these platforms now face and how it could determine their future.

Guest: David Yaffe-Bellany, a technology reporter for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • A clash between prediction markets and states has set off a furious political battle.
  • Donald Trump Jr.’s firm led a $1 billion funding round for Polymarket.

Photo: Eric Helgas for The New York Times

item.title: He Was Deported to a Country He’d Never Heard Of
item.description:
In its efforts to deport as many undocumented immigrants as possible, the Trump administration has increasingly relied on a highly controversial strategy: deporting people to countries they have no connection to.

Last week, a federal court ruled the practice to be illegal because it violated people’s right to due process. The administration challenged that ruling, and now it is in front of the Supreme Court.

Nicholas Casey tells the story of Roberto Mosquera, who moved to the United States from Cuba as a child. He has been held in the small country of Eswatini since July 2025.

Guest: Nicholas Casey, a staff writer at The New York Times Magazine who writes about geopolitics.

Background reading: 

  • He was deported to a country he’d never heard of. He may never go free.
  • How do you interview a deportee being held inside a maximum-security prison?

Photo: Moises Saman/Magnum, for The New York Times

item.title: The Best TV Shows of the 21st Century
item.description:
The turn of the century was the beginning of a new era in television: prestige TV for the masses. Today, television is where big stars and innovative creators go to marshal sizable budgets and tell meaningful stories.

Over recent months, our colleagues at The New York Times ran a survey, asking industry insiders — on-screen talent, writers, directors, producers, executives and others — to pick their top 10 television series of the last 26 years. We compiled their responses into a list, published this week, of the best TV of the 21st century.

In this episode of “The Sunday Daily,” The Times’s canon editor, Gilbert Cruz, and our chief TV critic, James Poniewozik, talk with our host Natalie Kitroeff about what made the list, and what didn’t.

 

On Today’s Episode

James Poniewozik is The New York Times’s chief TV critic.

Gilbert Cruz is the canon editor at The New York Times.

 

Background Reading

  • The 100 Best TV Shows of the 21st Century
  • The 100 Best TV Shows of the 21st Century: Cast Your Vote
  • The 100 Best TV Shows of the 21st Century: How Stars, Creators and Other TV Lovers Voted

item.title: The Life and, for Now, the Death of the Kennedy Center
item.description:
For 50 years, the Kennedy Center was a sprawling public home for opera, theater, jazz and free programs. Last week, it closed its doors for the time being.

Elizabeth Williamson traces how President Trump decided to take over and now shut down Washington’s biggest and most celebrated home for the arts.

Guest: Elizabeth Williamson, a feature writer for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Internal emails and documents demonstrate how President Trump broke the Kennedy Center.
  • The center removed a sculpture called “Blue” that had been a gift from the artist.

Photo: Salwan Georges for The New York Times

item.title: What Safeguarding Nukes Can Teach Us About Safeguarding A.I.
item.description:
Last night, President Trump welcomed Xi Jinping, China’s top leader, in a lavish ceremony as he arrived for two days of closely watched negotiations.

Artificial intelligence — and what, if any, role the countries should play in regulating it as concerns mount about its risks — is expected to be on the agenda.

David E. Sanger, a White House correspondent for The New York Times, explains how nuclear nonproliferation could be a model for how to protect humanity from technological catastrophe.

Guest: David E. Sanger, the White House and national security correspondent for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Mr. Trump greeted Mr. Xi for a state visit amid tensions.
  • Video: Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi face the A.I. race.
  • Analysis: As fears of A.I. catastrophe magnify, Washington stirs, but mostly slumbers.

Photo: Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: Health Trackers Are Everywhere. Do Babies Need Them, Too?
item.description:
More and more people are wearing technology in the form of fitness bands and smart rings. These devices track metrics such as heart rate, skin temperature and sleep. The latest frontier is health tech for babies — and it’s being supercharged by artificial intelligence.

Sapna Maheshwari shares her family’s experience with health tracking and discusses whether it’s helping people or just adding to their anxieties.

Guest: Sapna Maheshwari, a reporter covering new media companies for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Aw, it’s baby’s first A.I. surveillance system.
  • Will A.I. kill us? Can it hack my bank account? Your A.I. questions answered.

item.title: Trump Banned the Media. This Time, the Media Struck Back.
item.description:
For every day of Donald J. Trump’s presidency, there has been a camera from a major television network pointed at him. But on Monday, that all changed.

Zolan Kanno-Youngs and Michael M. Grynbaum discuss the face-off between the president and the press.

  • Michael M. Grynbaum, a media correspondent for The New York Times.

item.title: The Trump Administration Defangs the Endangered Species Act
item.description:
In its second term, the Trump administration has increased its efforts to undo environmental regulations. Last week, it became clear that the Endangered Species Act, one of America’s bedrock environmental laws, would be losing some of its most important protections.

Catrin Einhorn, who covers biodiversity, explains what is changing and what impact that could have on the country’s most vulnerable animals and ecosystems. 

Guest: Catrin Einhorn, a reporter covering biodiversity, climate and the environment for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • The Trump administration moved to gut a core protection of the Endangered Species Act last week.

item.title: How a 1,000-Year-Old Tapestry Took London by Storm
item.description:
For the first time in centuries, the Bayeux Tapestry — a nearly 1,000-year-old piece of embroidery that depicts the invasion of England by William the Conqueror in 1066 — is on display in Britain.

It was long said by art experts to be too fragile to move. But in a development that required geopolitical persuasion, this summer the tapestry made its way from Bayeux, France, to the British Museum in London.

When the first block of tickets went on sale, the British Museum said, over 80,000 people at a time waited online to buy them.

In this episode of the “Sunday Daily,” Alex Marshall, a culture reporter for The New York Times, talks with host Michael Barbaro about why this ancient piece of embroidery matters so much to the British public.

On Today’s Episode:

Alex Marshall is a European culture reporter for The New York Times, based in London.

Background Reading:

  • How to See a Bayeux Tapestry — Without Going to the British Museum
  • A Nation Gripped by ‘Bayeux Fever’ Finally Gets to See the Tapestry

Photo credit: Kin Cheung for Associated Press.

item.title: The Techno-Religion at the Center of the A.I. Debate
item.description:
Last week, a group of tech leaders called for putting guardrails on artificial intelligence. This week, these calls have been met by backlash from tech executives, lawmakers and President Trump, who liken those ringing the alarm to a doomsday cult.

Cade Metz, a technology reporter for The New York Times, explains where this criticism comes from and why it matters.

Guest: Cade Metz, a technology reporter for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • A.I. could possibly end humanity. How are humans supposed to process that?
  • “Recursive self-improvement” is an idea that terrifies A.I. doomsayers.
  • Top A.I. leaders called for slowing down A.I. development last week.

item.title: Why Gas Prices Just Keep Going Up
item.description:
About a month into the war with Iran, we spoke with Cameron Joudi, who owns a gas station in Florida, about how the conflict was reaching him at home. He recently reached out after seeing a 20-cent spike in gas prices in the span of just 24 hours.

Vivian Nereim, the Gulf bureau chief for The New York Times, tries to answer Mr. Joudi’s question: What’s driving rising oil prices?

Guest:

  • Cameron Joudi, the owner of a gas station in Florida.
  • Vivian Nereim, the Gulf bureau chief for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Listen to the interview with Mr. Joudi from March.
  • What’s driving up diesel prices? Energy chaos caused by two wars.
  • Gulf Arab states explore new options as U.S. bases fail to deter Iran.

item.title: 48 Days Until the Midterms: Is a Blue Wave Coming?
item.description:
As the general midterm elections begin, we take a look at where things stand. A new Times/Siena poll suggests that Democrats have a real shot at winning control of both chambers of Congress. But serious obstacles stand in their way, including a financial disadvantage.

item.title: The A.I. Researcher Whose Rebellion Is Changing Everything
item.description:
In recent days, Jacob Coxon, a researcher at the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, quit his job and posted warnings about the risks of the technology. That kicked off a crisis that culminated in a call by prominent leaders of the industry to slow down A.I. development.

item.title: The Good, the Bad and the Good-Bad (Movie)
item.description:
When it comes to movies we love, there are the artistic masterpieces and there are the foot-stomping crowd pleasers. But there’s another particular kind of beloved movie, the one that makes our friends groan, but that we rewatch incessantly; the one that we can quote line for line, even as we giggle at the actors’ performances; the one that we’d say is great, but that we might not say is good. These are the kinds of movies that Maya Salam, a pop culture writer at The New York Times, covers in her monthly column, The Good-Bad.

This episode is a celebration of good-bad movies, timed to the release of “Practical Magic 2,” the long-awaited sequel to the 1998 cult film that Salam called “a bubbling cauldron of plot holes and tones.” Our host Rachel Abrams talks to Salam about the joys of loving a movie despite (or because of) its flaws. Then, they’re joined by The Times’s canon editor, Gilbert Cruz, and Taffy Brodesser-Akner, a Times Magazine writer, to discuss the best of good-bad cinema.

On Today’s Episode:

Maya Salam covers pop culture for The New York Times.

Gilbert Cruz is the canon editor for The New York Times.

Taffy Brodesser-Akner is a features reporter for The New York Times Magazine.

Background Reading:

  • The Good-Bad
  • Why Loving Good-Bad Movies Feels All Good

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

This episode is a celebration of good-bad movies, timed to the release of “Practical Magic 2,” the long-awaited sequel to the 1998 cult film that Salam called “a bubbling cauldron of plot holes and tones.” Our host Rachel Abrams talks to Salam about the joys of loving a movie despite (or because of) its flaws. Then, they’re joined by The Times’s canon editor, Gilbert Cruz, and Taffy Brodesser-Akner, a Times Magazine writer, to discuss the best of good-bad cinema.

On Today’s Episode:

Maya Salam covers pop culture for The New York Times.

Gilbert Cruz is the canon editor for The New York Times.

Taffy Brodesser-Akner is a features reporter for The New York Times Magazine.

Background Reading:

  • The Good-Bad
  • Why Loving Good-Bad Movies Feels All Good

item.title: The Lives That 9/11 Keeps Taking
item.description:
In New York City this morning, the families of those killed at the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001, will gather for the 25th time to honor the dead one by one.

Among those at ground zero will be an array of city officials who assured the public that it was safe to return to Lower Manhattan just weeks after the attacks.

Today, Sally Goldenberg, a reporter who covers politics and government for The New York Times, and Dana Nelson, who attended school next to ground zero, reveal the 9/11 health crisis that has now claimed more lives than the terrorist attacks themselves.

Guest: Sally Goldenberg, a reporter covering New York City politics and government for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Documents suggest that New Yorkers were misled about air quality after 9/11.

Photo: Chang W. Lee/The New York Times

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: A Couple Breaks Up. Who Gets Custody of Their Embryos?
item.description:
As more people in the United States use I.V.F. to have children, embryos are being stored in fertility clinics across the country. It raises the question: What should happen to those embryos if a couple breaks up?

Caroline Kitchener, who covers families for The New York Times, tells the story of Erin Millender, who took a custody battle over frozen embryos to court after her husband revoked his consent to use them.

Guest: Caroline Kitchener, a New York Times reporter, writing about the American family.

Background reading: 

  • They started I.V.F., and then split. Now who gets custody of the embryos?

Photo: Kim Raff for The New York Times

item.title: Trump’s War on Mail-In Voting
item.description:
With only weeks to go before the midterms, President Trump has asked the Supreme Court to allow his administration’s plans to restrict voting by mail.

Nick Corasaniti, who covers national politics for The New York Times, walks us through Mr. Trump’s effort, the legal battle it touched off and the uncertainty it has created for local election officials and voters around the United States.

Guest: Nick Corasaniti, a New York Times reporter covering national politics, with a focus on voting and elections.

Background reading: 

  • The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court again to allow mail voting restrictions.
  • Where does the president’s effort to restrict mail voting stand?

item.title: ‘Buy Now, Pay Later’: A New Wave of Consumer Debt
item.description:
As people in the United States struggle with rising costs, they are increasingly turning to “buy now, pay later” loans for essentials such as rent and groceries.

Stacey Cowley, a business reporter for The New York Times, explains the draw and the hidden risks of the loan model.

Guest: Stacy Cowley, a business reporter at The New York Times, with a focus on consumer finance.

Background reading: 

  • “Buy now, pay later” lenders have pitched loans for needs like electricity and rent.
  • They got to live a life of luxury. Then came the fine print.

item.title: Classical Music Is in Crisis. Gustavo Dudamel Is Here to Save It.
item.description:
This week marks the start of the Gustavo Dudamel era in New York.

The superstar conductor was just 28 when he became the musical director of the Los Angeles Philharmonic in 2009. A native of Venezuela and a product of its El Sistema musical training program, Dudamel quickly established himself not just as a great conductor, but also as a cultural force of nature. In his time in Los Angeles, he expanded the Philharmonic’s repertoire, created a successful youth outreach program, won prestigious awards and ingratiated himself with Hollywood elite.

Now, after 17 years in Los Angeles, Dudamel is taking the helm at one of the world’s most famous and storied orchestras: the New York Philharmonic. It’s a job once held by Leonard Bernstein, and Dudamel is hoping to follow in Bernstein’s footsteps to make the Philharmonic and the music that it plays a bigger part of the pop culture landscape.

On today’s episode, Joshua Barone, who covers classical music for The Times, discusses Dudamel, what he’s accomplished and the high hopes for his tenure with the New York Philharmonic.


Music Featured (in order of appearance, all conducted by Gustavo Dudamel):

  • Johann Strauss, Tik-Tak Polka, Polka Schnell, Op. 365, Weiner Philharmoniker (Sony Music Entertainment)
  • Dmitri Shostakovich, Festive Overture, Op. 96, Simón Bolívar Youth Orchestra (Deutsche Grammophon)
  • Gustav Mahler, Symphony No. 5 in C-Sharp Minor IV. Adagietto, Berlin Philharmonic (Berlin Philharmonic Recordings)
  • Antonin Dvorak, Symphony No. 8 in G Major, Op. 88, B. 163, III. Allegretto grazioso- Molto vivace, Los Angeles Philharmonic (Deutsche Grammophon)
  • John Williams, “The Imperial March” (From “Star Wars: Episode V — The Empire Strikes Back”), Los Angeles Philharmonic (UMG Recordings, Inc)
  • John Adams, “En un Día de Amor Yo Bajé Hasta la Tierra,” The Gospel According to the Other Mary, Los Angeles Master Chorale and Los Angeles Philharmonic (Deutsche Grammophon)
  • Gabriela Ortiz, “Kauyumari,” Los Angeles Philharmonic (Platoon)
  • Ludwig Beethoven, Symphony No. 7 in A Major, Op. 92, IV. Allegro con brio, Simón Bolívar Youth Orchestra (Deutsche Grammophon)
  • Thomas Adès, “XII. The Thieves — devoured by reptiles,” Dante, Los Angeles Master Chorale and Los Angeles Philharmonic (Nonesuch Records)
  • Ludwig Beethoven, Symphony No. 5 in C Minor, Op. 67: I. Allegro con brio, Simón Bolívar Youth Orchestra (Deutsche Grammophon)
  • Ludwig Beethoven, Symphony No. 5 in C Minor, Op. 67: I. Allegro con brio, Simón Bolívar Symphony Orchestra (self-released)
  • Leonard Bernstein, “End Credits” and “The Dance at the Gym: Mambo,” from “West Side Story” (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack), Los Angeles Philharmonic and New York Philharmonic (Hollywood Records)

On Today’s Episode:

Joshua Barone is an editor for the Culture section of The New York Times who works on classical music and dance coverage. He also writes criticism about classical music and opera.

Background Reading:

  • Gustavo Dudamel’s Long Goodbye to L.A., and Long Hello to New York

  • What Makes Superstar Conductor Gustavo Dudamel So Good?

    Photo Credit: James Estrin/ The New York Times

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: The Intertwined Legacies of Gloria Steinem and Dolly Parton
item.description:
Gloria Steinem, the feminist icon and co-founder of Ms. magazine, died on Wednesday at her home in Manhattan. Her death came as many were still grieving the loss of another iconic woman: Dolly Parton.

On paper, the connections between the two women seem superficial, but for the Times Magazine writer Susan Dominus, the relationship between their lives and impact is inescapable.

Guest: 

  • Susan Dominus, a staff writer at The New York Times Magazine.
  • Letty Cottin Pogrebin, a writer and pioneer of the feminist movement who was part of the team that founded Ms. magazine with Gloria Steinem.

Background reading: 

  • In “9 to 5,” Dolly Parton put a friendly face on feminism.
  • Gloria Steinem, the personification of the women’s movement, died at 92.

Photo: Robin Platzer/Getty Images

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: A.I. Is Outsmarting Its Creators
item.description:
From the start, the greatest fear for those developing artificial intelligence was that their creations would go rogue to act in unauthorized and dangerous ways. Some researchers now say it has happened.

Kevin Roose, a technology columnist for The New York Times, explains what this means for his own dwindling sense of techno-optimism.

Guest: Kevin Roose, a technology columnist for The New York Times and a host of the Times tech podcast, “Hard Fork.”

Background reading: 

  • Anatomy of an autonomous attack: five alarming A.I. capabilities.
  • A previous episode of “The Daily” looked at the debate in Silicon Valley over the right way to build artificial intelligence.

item.title: The Fight for the West Bank
item.description:
Over the past year, there has been an increase in violence in the West Bank. Israeli settlers have terrorized Palestinians, set fire to their property, uprooted their olive groves and stolen their animals in an effort to drive them off their land.

Rachel Abrams speaks to Loui Ridi, a Palestinian American in the West Bank, about the settlers who have arrived at his doorstep.

Guest: Loui Ridi, a Palestinian American in the West Bank.

Background reading: 

  • With the world distracted by war, extremist settlers have intensified their attacks in the West Bank.
  • An assault by Israeli settlers on Palestinians last week drew sharp rebukes.

item.title: How a Teenager Found Undiagnosed Brain Injuries in the Military
item.description:
Warning: this episode contains mentions of suicide.

New reporting has found that the impact of rough sea waves on rescue-boat crews in the Coast Guard can lead to long-term effects, including traumatic brain injury.

Dave Philipps, who reports about veterans for The New York Times, explains the significant blind spot in the Coast Guard and talks about how a teenager helped expose this widespread danger. 

Guest: Dave Philipps, who reports about war, the military and veterans for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Rescue-boat crews show signs of brain injuries.
  • After an article by The Times, the Coast Guard vowed to protect crews from brain injuries caused by rough seas.

Photo: Ruth Fremson/The New York Times

item.title: How Flock Cameras Took Over America
item.description:
This summer, Fernando Alfonso, the Texas editor for The New York Times, got in a car with a man named Philip. They drove around the suburban streets of Dallas searching for traffic cameras — not for a red-light camera, or a speed-trap camera, but something new, an automatic license-plate reader made by a company called Flock.

Law enforcement officials say these cameras are essential to fighting crime, but Phillip and people like him, who have located 100,000 flock cameras all over the country, see them as something else: the beginnings of a surveillance state.

Today, Kashmir Hill, a technology and privacy writer at The New York Times, discusses the company behind the cameras and the mounting backlash.

Guest: Kashmir Hill, a technology and privacy writer at The New York Times.

Background reading: One thing Texan liberals and conservatives agree on: They don’t want cameras trained on their cars.

Photo: Desiree Rios for The New York Times

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: Who Will Rule the 2026 U.S. Open?
item.description:
The U.S. Open, the final tournament of the tennis season, is getting underway. The world’s best players are heading to the U.S.T.A. Billie Jean King National Tennis Center in Queens, N.Y., to battle it out for the chance to play a championship match at Arthur Ashe Stadium, the largest tennis arena in the world.

The players come freighted with great expectations, previous victories and defeats, aches and pains, personal dramas and professional rivalries, all of which they will carry with them out on the court when they play. Tennis is a game that exposes a lot about its players, which is one of the things that makes it so beloved around the world.

In this episode of the “Sunday Daily,” the host Natalie Kitroeff talks with Matthew Futterman, a senior tennis writer for The Athletic and the author of “The Cruelest Game: Chasing Greatness in Professional Tennis,” about this year’s crop of players. They’ll dig into the biggest rivalries and dramas brewing in the tournament ahead.

On Today’s Episode:

Matthew Futterman, a senior tennis writer for The Athletic, and the author of “The Cruelest Game: Chasing Greatness in Professional Tennis.”

Background Reading:

“U.S. Open Men’s Title Contenders: Jannik Sinner Cut, Carlos Alcaraz In and a U.S. Man’s Big Chance?”

Photo credit: Al Bello/Getty Images. 

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: Lindsay Clancy Is on Trial. So Is Postpartum Psychosis.
item.description:
Warning: this episode mentions suicide.

The trial of Lindsay Clancy, a mother who is being tried for the killings of her three young children, has captivated the country for weeks. It has also raised difficult questions about how we treat postpartum women who are in crisis.

Ellen Barry, a New York Times reporter who has been covering the trial, takes us inside the courtroom and explains the stakes of the outcome.

Guest: Ellen Barry, a reporter covering mental health for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • What we know about the trial of Lindsay Clancy for her children’s deaths.
  • Why the Lindsay Clancy case is dividing Americans.
  • How to understand the wide range of sympathy for a mother on trial for murder.

Photo: Pool photo by Greg Derr

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: A Historic Settlement Over Social Media Addiction
item.description:
Meta, the world’s biggest social media company, reached a multibillion-dollar legal settlement on Wednesday over claims that its technology was addictive to children.

The company agreed to impose major changes to how minors use its products.

Cecilia Kang, a technology reporter for The New York Times, explains why a company that almost never backs down finally cut a deal, and whether this will start a new era of accountability for Big Tech.

Guest: Cecilia Kang, a reporter covering technology and regulatory policy for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Meta will pay up to $17.1 billion over claims of social media addiction.
  • A movement to restrict social media for children has taken hold globally.

Photo: Jason Henry for The New York Times

For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/thedaily. Transcripts of each episode will be made available by the next workday.

item.title: The Stunning Rise of the Democratic Socialists of America
item.description:
This summer, the Democratic Socialists of America have mounted their biggest and most successful attempt yet to redefine the Democratic Party. They have defeated its candidates in primary after primary from coast to coast.

As its electoral success grows, the organization is confronting big, unresolved questions about what it stands for and what level of compromise is required to become a lasting political force.

Charles Homans, who talked to more than 30 D.S.A. candidates, organizers, members and volunteers across the countries, discusses the rise and limitations of the D.S.A. 

Guest: Charles Homans writes about national politics for The New York Times and The Times Magazine.

Background reading: 

  • Moderates see socialists as a threat to the Democratic Party. Socialists agree.

Photo: Dave Sanders and Jamie Kelter Davis for The New York Times; Joe Raedle/Getty Images

item.content:encoded:
This summer, the Democratic Socialists of America have mounted their biggest and most successful attempt yet to redefine the Democratic Party. They have defeated its candidates in primary after primary from coast to coast.

As its electoral success grows, the organization is confronting big, unresolved questions about what it stands for and what level of compromise is required to become a lasting political force.

Charles Homans, who talked to more than 30 D.S.A. candidates, organizers, members and volunteers across the countries, discusses the rise and limitations of the D.S.A. 

Guest: Charles Homans writes about national politics for The New York Times and The Times Magazine.

Background reading: 

  • Moderates see socialists as a threat to the Democratic Party. Socialists agree.

item.title: Canada Is Done With Trump
item.description:
In a dramatic decision, the prime minister of Canada abruptly cut off negotiations with the United States, delivering the message to President Trump that he would rather engage in an ugly trade war than submit to an unfair deal.

Matina Stevis-Gridneff, the Canada bureau chief for The New York Times, explains how the two countries reached a breaking point and describes Canada’s plan to withstand economic warfare.

item.title: Natalie Harp’s Devotion to Trump
item.description:
Natalie Harp is a constant presence at President Trump’s side. She’s a 35-year-old gatekeeper, deciding much of what he sees. She stays up late with him to draft his social media posts and even texts with world leaders on his behalf.

Today, Maggie Haberman, a White House correspondent for The New York Times, covers what we know about Trump’s closest aide and why people inside and outside the White House are questioning her devotion to the president.

Guest: Maggie Haberman, a White House correspondent for The New York Times.

item.title: Think Baseball Is Boring? The Savannah Bananas Are Here to Fix That.
item.description:
Jesse and Emily Cole created the Savannah Bananas with a simple mission in mind: to make baseball as entertaining as possible. They introduced some innovations to America’s pastime, including twerking umpires, stilt-walking pitchers and TikTok-ready choreographed dance numbers. They tinkered with the rules of baseball, making a game that was shorter and faster, with plenty of opportunities for fan engagement. The result? A sports sensation. In the 10 years since its founding, the team has become one of the most popular sports organizations in the world, reaching tens of millions of fans online, with a waiting list of millions of others hoping to see a game in person.

For many, the Bananas are the ultimate sports success story, one that shows a path forward for teams and leagues concerned about fan retention in an era of shortened attention spans and endless entertainment options. But others take a less rosy view of the Bananas and their hyper-energetic brand of baseball, seeing them as an existential threat to a game that fans have loved for more than a hundred years.

On today’s show, our host Natalie Kitroeff talks with Jonathan Abrams, a Times reporter who covers culture news, about the Bananas phenomenon, and then heads to a Banana Ball game to see things for herself.

 

On Today's Episode

Jonathan Abrams is a reporter for The New York Times covering national culture news.

 

Background Reading

A Broadway Star Is the Savannah Bananas’ Phantom of the Bullpen

As Savannah Bananas pursue ‘a billion fans,’ are they real competition for MLB?

 

Photo: Al Bello/Getty Images

item.title: When Private Equity Comes for Your Favorite Team
item.description:
Last week, the owner of the Los Angeles Lakers announced he was selling the basketball team for $12.5 billion — the highest price ever paid for a professional sports team. The deal has shocked the sports world and drawn new attention to a growing trend: Big groups of investors have been buying up professional sports teams as the franchises chase skyrocketing valuations.

Today, Pablo Torre, the host of “Pablo Torre Finds Out,” explains the deal and how big money is transforming our relationship with the sports we love.

Guest: Pablo Torre, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist and the host of “Pablo Torre Finds Out.”

Background reading: 

  • The deal for the Los Angeles Lakers valued the team at a record $12.5 billion, eclipsing the $10 billion paid for the franchise just last year.
  • The transaction for the Lakers reflects the huge profit potential of major sports franchises.

Photo: Logan Riely/NBAE, via Getty Images

item.title: Who Moves Up, and Who's Pushed Out, in Pete Hegseth's Military
item.description:
For the past 18 months, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has remade the top ranks of the U.S. military — dismissing or sidelining many whose rise he believes was aided by D.E.I. and replacing them with officers who fit his definition of merit. In the process, many argue he’s prioritizing loyalty to him and his ideas over loyalty to the military itself.

Today, Greg Jaffe, a New York Times reporter who covers the Pentagon and the U.S. military, takes us inside the hiring and firing for a single job that has become a case study for Hegseth’s approach.

Guest: Greg Jaffe, a reporter covering the Pentagon and the U.S. military for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Before he was picked to lead the Navy, Adm. Daryl Caudle found ways to signal his support for Mr. Hegseth’s anti-diversity goals.
  • Mr. Hegseth fired the Navy’s top officer, Adm. Lisa Franchetti, who spent roughly half of her 40-year career at sea, commanding a destroyer, two carrier strike groups and the U.S. Sixth Fleet.

Photo: Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times

item.title: El Niño Is Back. And Worse Than Ever.
item.description:
The global chaos agent known as El Niño is back, and this year it’s already on track to be, by far, the strongest and most severe on record, wreaking havoc on weather across the world.

Today, Chico Harlan, the global climate reporter for The New York Times, goes over El Niño’s history, its inner workings and its increasingly destructive fallout.

Guest: Chico Harlan, the global climate correspondent for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • El Niño, the Pacific climate shift that comes around once or twice a decade, is back, warming tropical oceans and setting off consequences worldwide.
  • It’s expected to peak later this year but is already causing dry spells and crop failures on three continents.

Photo: Bay Ismoyo/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

item.title: What Went Wrong on the U.S.S. Lincoln?
item.description:
For the past two weeks, family members of sailors have been raising alarms about the conditions aboard the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln, which has a crew of about 5,000 and has been at sea for almost nine months straight.

Today, John Ismay, a New York Times reporter who covers the Pentagon with a focus on armed conflict and the defense industry, discusses what went wrong on the ship and how it could affect the U.S. military’s ability to fight wars.

Guest: John Ismay, a New York Times reporter who covers the Pentagon with a focus on armed conflict and the defense industry.

Background reading: 

  • The U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln has been deployed for nearly nine months. Members of Congress are worried about the crew’s well-being.
  • Admiral Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, acknowledged the difficulty of the carrier’s lengthy deployment but said mental health issues were lower than on other vessels.

Photo: Jason Waite/Agence France-Presse, via Navy Office of Information

Today, John Ismay, a New York Times reporter who covers the Pentagon with a focus on armed conflict and the defense industry, discusses what went wrong on the ship and how it could affect the U.S. military’s ability to fight wars.

Guest: John Ismay, a New York Times reporter who covers the Pentagon with a focus on armed conflict and the defense industry.

Background reading: 

  • The U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln has been deployed for nearly nine months. Members of Congress are worried about the crew’s well-being.
  • Admiral Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, acknowledged the difficulty of the carrier’s lengthy deployment but said mental health issues were lower than on other vessels.

Photo: Jason Waite/Agence France-Presse, via Navy Office of Information

item.title: Luigi Mangione’s High-Risk Legal Strategy
item.description:
In the two years since a masked man shot and killed a health care executive, the national spotlight has turned to the primary suspect, Luigi Mangione. The overwhelming evidence has pointed to his guilt, and the question on most minds has been: What might the defense of one of the most famous murder suspects in America look like?

At a hearing on Friday, we got our first glimpse at an answer, one that appears to include a full-throated embrace of his guilt.

Today, Benjamin Weiser, a reporter covering the justice system for The New York Times, and Hurubie Meko, a criminal justice reporter for The Times, discuss the risky defense strategy and why an admission of guilt might be Mr. Mangione’s best bet.

Guests: 

  • Benjamin Weiser, a reporter covering the justice system for The New York Times.
  • Hurubie Meko, a criminal justice reporter for The New York Times.

Background reading: Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty to federal charges, and still faces a state case.

Photo: Pool photo by David Dee Delgado

item.title: What Makes a Killer Thriller?
item.description:
The New York Times Book Review recently released its list of the 50 best thrillers of the 21st century.

To put it together, the team asked almost 300 authors and other experts to vote for the best heart-thumping, page-turning, white knuckle reads published since 2000.

In this episode of “The Sunday Daily,” Natalie Kitroeff talks with the Times thrillers columnist, Sarah Lyall, about how the list came together. Then, Natalie speaks with one of the greatest thriller writers of this century — with four books featured on the list — the author Tana French.

On Today’s Episode:

Sarah Lyall writes a monthly thrillers column for The New York Times.

Tana French is the author of many best-selling books, including “In the Woods,” “The Searcher,” “The Likeness” and “The Witch Elm.”

Background Reading:

The 50 Best Thrillers of the 21st Century

item.title: The Secret Spy Network Feeding Russia’s War Machine
item.description:
Ukraine is running desperately low on interceptor missiles, leaving its cities and people nearly defenseless against Russian missile and drone attacks. How Russia has been able to sustain those attacks has been a mystery — until now.

Today, Jane Bradley, a Britain-based investigative reporter for The New York Times, explains her investigation into the spy network that has allowed the Kremlin to keep this war going.

Guest: Jane Bradley, a Britain-based investigative reporter for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • A Russian spy who used the Aeroflot office in Tokyo to smuggle high-tech weapon components into Russia has left Japan after a Times report.
  • Operating out of a Tokyo high-rise, a military intelligence unit takes advantage of Japan’s weak espionage laws to find the high-tech equipment that Russia needs to wage war.

Photo: Chang W. Lee/The New York Times

item.title: Are The Democratic Socialists Winning or Losing?
item.description:
This week, Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist running for governor in Wisconsin, suffered an upset after a double-digit lead in the polls. Last week, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive, pulled off a stunning victory in Michigan against his well-funded opponent.

Nate Cohn, the chief political analyst for The New York Times, makes sense of what happened in Wisconsin and Michigan, and what it might tell us about the future of the Democratic Party.

Guest: Nate Cohn, the chief political analyst for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Dr. El-Sayed’s triumph against an establishment-backed candidate in Michigan was a big win for the left.
  • Ms. Hong’s defeat in Wisconsin defied expectations and may have shown that the democratic socialist wave cannot reach beyond urban centers.

Photo: Nick Hagen for The New York Times

item.title: All the President’s Planes
item.description:
When President Trump left Turkey, the White House said publicly that he was boarding the old Air Force One — but that plane was a decoy. In a highly elaborate escape plan prompted by a credible Iranian threat, Trump was secretly moved through a catering cart to a military aircraft, leaving passengers unknowingly flying on the decoy plane.

Today, Maggie Haberman, a White House correspondent for The New York Times, details the operation’s risks and what it reveals about how seriously the administration views the danger to the president.

Guest: Maggie Haberman, a White House correspondent for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • President Trump hid in an airport catering container and was transported to a military jet for a secret flight out of country.

Photo: Doug Mills/The New York Times

item.title: The U.S. Missile Stockpile Is Dangerously Low
item.description:
As the fighting with Iran has dragged on, American forces have been burning through their weapons, creating a shortage of munitions that is leaving the United States and its allies in the region much more vulnerable.

Today, Eric Schmitt, a national security correspondent for The New York Times, explains why Washington is running out of key missiles so quickly, and how the munitions shortage might affect the safety of U.S. troops and the Trump administration’s efforts to end the war.

Guest: Eric Schmitt, a national security correspondent for The New York Times.

Background reading: The war in Iran has depleted U.S. weapons stockpiles, resulting in a significant erosion of firepower.

Photo: Martin Divisek/EPA, via Shutterstock

item.title: Why Adults Are Getting Cancer at a Younger Age
item.description:
For years, cancer has been seen as a disease people mostly get when they’re older. That seems to be changing as more young people are getting cancer than ever before.

Today, Nina Agrawal, a health reporter for The New York Times, explains what scientists are learning about the factors driving the rise and what it means for a generation of young cancer survivors.

Guest: Nina Agrawal, a health reporter for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Hundreds of New York Times readers shared their experiences with early-onset cancers. Here are seven of their stories.
  • Research is starting to offer clues about why more than a dozen types of cancer have increased among people under 50 in the past decade.

Photo: Leah Nash for The New York Times

item.title: Is 'Gentle Parenting' Ruining French Children?
item.description:
“Traditional” French parenting is built on a foundation of firm boundaries, strictness and punishment for misbehavior. Within these rules, children are also allowed freedom and autonomy, which some say results in both well-behaved children and stress-free parents.

In recent years, though, American-style “gentle” or “positive” parenting has gained a toehold in the country, unsettling decades of orthodoxy about the best way to raise a French child. It has prompted a fierce debate, with both sides accusing the other of being harmful.

In today’s episode, Madeleine Schwartz, a journalist who lives in Paris, talks with Michael Barbaro about the dispute over parenting styles in France and what it says about the eternal search for the “right” way to raise children.

On Today’s Episode:

Madeleine Schwartz is a journalist and editor in Paris.

Background Reading:

Did American-Style ‘Gentle Parenting’ Spoil French Children?

Art Credit: Illustration by Kimberly Elliott
